metadata.title: On upper bounds of frieze patterns

extraction_notes.note: Section 2 is titled 'Proof of Theorem 1' but holds definitions, lemmas and environment proofs, so it was not made a single section-wide proof node; Theorem 1's parts are claims ClP1/ClP2 proved by PP1 (reduction to Prop 2.5) and PP6.
theorem or remark: cited facts stated only loosely (folding of C_n from A_{2n-1}; Caldero-Chapoton realisation); kept as external theorems at low confidence.
Muller's explicit upper bound for u_A and the Lean4 formalisation note are only mentioned, not stated, so no node; the figures (friezes of width 1 and 2) are not nodes.

nodes.name: Coxeter frieze pattern
differentia: consisting entirely of positive integers satisfying the so-called {\it diamond rule}
nodes.statement_short: A width-$n$ frieze is an $(n+2)$-row staggered array of positive integers with $ad=1+bc$ on every diamond.

nodes.name: Coxeter frieze array
nodes.statement:
\begin{array}{ccccccccccccccc}
            \cdots &   & 1 &   & 1 &   & 1 &     & \cdots &   &   &   &   &   &\\
              & \cdots &   & a_1 &   & b_1 &   & c_1 &     & \cdots &   &   &   &   &\\
              &   & \cdots &   & a_2 &   & b_2 &   & c_2 &     & \cdots &   &   &   &\\
              &   &   &   &   & \ddots &   & \ddots &   & \ddots &      &   &   &   &\\
              &   &   &   & \cdots &   & a_n &   & b_n &   & c_n &    & \cdots &   &\\
              &   &   &   &   & \cdots &   & 1 &   & 1 &   & 1 &     & \cdots &\\
        \end{array}
nodes.statement_short: Shape of a frieze: rows of 1s bounding $n$ rows of entries $a_i,b_i,c_i,\dots$.
nodes.label: eq:Coxeter

nodes.name: Caldero-Chapoton realisation of friezes via cluster algebras
nodes.statement:
One important generalisation was given in the mid-2000s, when P. Caldero and F. Chapoton \cite{CC06} realised frieze patterns of a given width n 
    as evaluations of distinguished ring homomorphisms  
    on all cluster variables in the cluster algebra (with trivial coefficients) of type $A_n$, thus unveiling the cluster algebra nature of frieze patterns.
nodes.statement_short: Width-$n$ friezes are evaluations of ring homomorphisms on cluster variables of the type $A_n$ cluster algebra.

nodes.name: Frieze pattern of type A (Assem-Reutenauer-Smith)
nodes.statement_short: A frieze of Cartan type $A$ is a positive-integer map on $\{1..n\}\times\mathbb Z$ obeying the generalised exchange relation.
nodes.label: def:frieze

nodes.name: Type A_n recovers Coxeter friezes
nodes.statement:
When $A=(a_{i,j})$ is the so-called standard Cartan matrix of type $A_n$ (see \S \ref{ss:Cartan}), one recovers (Coxeter) frieze patterns of width $n$ by placing 
    each tuple $(f(1,m), \ldots, f(n,m)), m \in \mathbb{Z}$ in the $m^{\rm th}$ North-West to South-East diagonal in \eqref{eq:Coxeter}.
nodes.statement_short: For the standard $A_n$ Cartan matrix, Definition 1.1 gives Coxeter friezes of width $n$, diagonal by diagonal.

nodes.name: Finiteness of friezes iff finite type
nodes.statement: Remarkably, the set ${\rm Frieze}(A)$ is finite if and only if $A$ is of ``finite type", i.e. $A$ is positive definite (c.f. \cite{FZ:II,GM:finite}).
conclusions: the set ${\rm Frieze}(A)$ is finite if and only if $A$ is of ``finite type", i.e. $A$ is positive definite
equivalent_conditions: $A$ is of ``finite type", i.e. $A$ is positive definite

nodes.name: Conway-Coxeter bijection and Catalan count
nodes.statement: A first step in this direction was achieved by Coxeter and Conway \cite{CC73}, who constructed a beautiful bijection from ${\rm Frieze}(A_n)$ to the set of triangulations of the regular $(n+3)$-gon, whereby $c(A_n) = C_{n+1} = \frac{1}{n+2} \binom{2n+2}{n+1}$, {\it the $(n+1)^{\rm st}$ Catalan number}.
nodes.statement_short: Friezes of type $A_n$ biject with triangulations of the $(n+3)$-gon, so there are Catalan-many.

nodes.name: Number of friezes of types E_7 and E_8
nodes.statement:
At the time of writing,  
    $c(E_7)$ and $c(E_8)$ are not known (but see \cite{FP:Dn,GM:finite} for conjectural values).

nodes.name: Periodicity of friezes of finite type
nodes.statement:
Keeping with the assumption that $A$ is of finite type, Coxeter \cite{Coxeter1971} proved in type $A_n$ and \cite{Keller:periodicity} proved in general that every $f \in {\rm Frieze}(A)$ is periodic in the second component, i.e. there exists $N_A$ such that 
    \[
        f(i,m) = f(i,m+N_A), \quad \forall i, \forall m.
    \]
conclusions: every $f \in {\rm Frieze}(A)$ is periodic in the second component
nodes.statement_short: Every frieze of finite type is periodic in $m$ with some period $N_A$.

nodes.name: Maximum frieze value u_A
nodes.statement_short: $u_A$ is the largest entry over all friezes of type $A$.

nodes.name: Definition of u_A
nodes.statement: u_A := \max (f (i,m) : f \in {\rm Frieze}(A), i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}, m \in \mathbb{Z}).

nodes.name: Maximum values of frieze patterns of types A_n and C_n
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a Cartan matrix of finite type. Then, 
    \begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(1)]
        \item if $A$ is of type $A_n$, then $u_A = F_{n+2}$; and
        \item if $A$ is of type $C_n$ then $u_A = F_{2n+1}$, 
    \end{enumerate}
    where $F_n$ is the $n^{\rm th}$ Fibonacci number, defined by $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a Cartan matrix of finite type.
conclusions: if $A$ is of type $A_n$, then $u_A = F_{n+2}$
if $A$ is of type $C_n$ then $u_A = F_{2n+1}$
nodes.statement_short: The maximum entry of a frieze is the Fibonacci number $F_{n+2}$ in type $A_n$ and $F_{2n+1}$ in type $C_n$.
nodes.label: mainthm

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (1): u_{A_n} = F_{n+2}
nodes.statement: if $A$ is of type $A_n$, then $u_A = F_{n+2}$; and

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (2): u_{C_n} = F_{2n+1}
nodes.statement: if $A$ is of type $C_n$ then $u_A = F_{2n+1}$,

nodes.name: Symmetrisable generalised Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
A {\it symmetrisable generalised Cartan matrix} is an $n \times n$ integral matrix 
$A = (a_{i, j})_{i, j = 1, \ldots, n}$ such that 

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $a_{i ,i} = 2$ for all $i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$,
    \item $a_{i, j} \leq 0$ for all $i, j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $i \neq j$, with $a_{i,j} = 0$ if and only if $a_{j,i}=0$, and
    \item there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ with positive integers on the diagonal such that $DA$ is symmetric.
\end{enumerate}
A symmetrisable generalised Cartan matrix is said to be of {\it finite type} if it is positive definite. If there exists a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns of $A$ such that $A$ is block diagonal, we say that $A$ is {\it decomposable}. If not, we say that $A$ is {\it indecomposable}.
differentia: $a_{i, j} \leq 0$ for all $i, j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $i \neq j$, with $a_{i,j} = 0$ if and only if $a_{j,i}=0$
there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ with positive integers on the diagonal such that $DA$ is symmetric
nodes.statement_short: Integral matrix with 2s on the diagonal, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and a symmetrising diagonal; finite type means positive definite.
nodes.label: def:cartan

nodes.name: Cartan-Killing classification of finite type Cartan matrices
nodes.statement: It is well-known that indecomposable Cartan matrices of finite type are classified into four classical series $A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n$ and five exceptional types labeled as $G_2, F_4, E_6, E_7, E_8$.
also_stated_at: It is well known that such a classification can be broken down into 4 infinite families (denoted $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$ and $D_n$) and five exceptional types $G_2,F_4,E_6, E_7$ and $E_8$.
assumptions: indecomposable Cartan matrices of finite type
conclusions: are classified into four classical series $A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n$ and five exceptional types labeled as $G_2, F_4, E_6, E_7, E_8$

nodes.name: Standard Cartan matrix of type A_n
nodes.statement:
In this article, the {\it standard Cartan matrix of type $A_n$} is the $n\times n$ integer matrix
\begin{equation} A_n = \left(\begin{array}{cccccc} 2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
-1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 2 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots& \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 2 & -1\\
0 & 0 & 0& \cdots & -1 & 2\end{array}\right).
\end{equation}

nodes.statement:
A_n = \left(\begin{array}{cccccc} 2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
-1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 2 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots& \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 2 & -1\\
0 & 0 & 0& \cdots & -1 & 2\end{array}\right).
nodes.label: eq:Cartan-An

nodes.name: Standard Cartan matrix of type C_n
nodes.statement:
Similarly, the {\it standard Cartan matrix of type $C_n$} is the $n\times n$ integer matrix
\begin{equation} C_n = \left(\begin{array}{cccccc} 2 & -1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
-1 & 2 & -1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 2 & \cdots & 0 & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots& \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 2 & -2\\
0 & 0 & 0& \cdots & -1 & 2\end{array}\right).
\end{equation}

\vdots & \vdots & \vdots& \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 2 & -2\\
0 & 0 & 0& \cdots & -1 & 2\end{array}\right).
nodes.label: eq:Cartan-Cn

nodes.name: Folding of A_{2n-1} to C_n
nodes.statement:
It is well-known (see \cite{FP:Dn}) that 
$C_n$ is a ``folding" of type $A_{2n-1}$ via a certain automorphism $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: $C_n$ is obtained from $A_{2n-1}$ by folding along an automorphism $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Frieze pattern of type A_n
nodes.statement:
A \emph{frieze pattern of type $A_n$} is a map $f:\{1,\dots,n\}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that for all $i\in \{1,\dots,n\}$ and all $m\in \mathbb{Z}$, we have
    \begin{equation} f(i,m)f(i,m+1) = 1 + f(i+1,m)f(i-1,m+1),
    \end{equation}
    where by convention $f(0,m)=f(n+1,m):=1$ for all $m\in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.label: def:friezeAn

nodes.name: A frieze pattern of type A_5
nodes.label: ex:friezeA5

nodes.name: m-th diagonal of a frieze
nodes.statement: For each $m\in \mathbb{Z}$, the $n$-tuple $(f(1,m),\dots, f(n,m))$ is called the $m$th \emph{diagonal} of $f$.

nodes.name: Diagonal of a frieze pattern
nodes.statement: Conversely, an $n$-tuple of positive integers $(a_1, \ldots , a_n)$ is called a {\it diagonal of a frieze pattern} if there exists a frieze pattern $f$ and an $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $a_i = f (i,m)$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$.
differentia: there exists a frieze pattern $f$ and an $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $a_i = f (i,m)$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$

nodes.name: A frieze is determined by any diagonal
nodes.statement: By recursively solving (\ref{eqn:diamond}) with respect to the (lexicographical) total order on $\{1,\dots,n\}\times \mathbb{Z}$, a frieze pattern is uniquely determined by any one of its diagonals.
conclusions: a frieze pattern is uniquely determined by any one of its diagonals

nodes.name: Conway-Coxeter divisibility criterion for diagonals
conclusions: is a diagonal of a frieze pattern if and only if
equivalent_conditions: is a diagonal of a frieze pattern
nodes.statement_short: A positive tuple is a frieze diagonal iff each entry divides the sum of its neighbours (with $a_0=a_{n+1}=1$).
nodes.label: friezeFlute

nodes.name: Divisibility condition (*)
nodes.statement:
\tag{$\ast$}
        \text{for all } i \in \{1,\dots,n\},\quad a_i \text{ divides } a_{i-1} + a_{i+1},
nodes.label: cond:flute

nodes.name: Reduction of Theorem 1 (1) to Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: In light of Lemma \ref{friezeFlute}, proving statement (1) of Theorem \ref{mainthm} reduces to proving the following proposition.
nodes.statement_short: By the divisibility criterion, bounding frieze entries reduces to bounding tuples satisfying (*).

nodes.name: Fibonacci bound on tuples satisfying (*)
nodes.statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. The following statements hold.
    \begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(1)]
        \item If $(a_1,\ldots, a_n)$ satisfies  {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, then $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$.
        
        \item If $n$ is even, the $n$-tuple 
    $$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n},  F_{n+2}, F_{n+1}, F_{n-1},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}.
    
        \item If $n$ is odd, the $n$-tuple 
     $$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n+1},  F_{n+2}, F_{n}, F_{n-2},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
     satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}.
    \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$
satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}

$$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n},  F_{n+2}, F_{n+1}, F_{n-1},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}

$$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n+1},  F_{n+2}, F_{n}, F_{n-2},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
     satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}
$a_i \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$

$$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n},  F_{n+2}, F_{n+1}, F_{n-1},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}

$$\left(F_4, F_6,\dots, F_{n+1},  F_{n+2}, F_{n}, F_{n-2},\dots, F_5, F_3\right)$$
     satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}

nodes.statement_short: Entries of tuples satisfying (*) are at most $F_{n+2}$, and explicit Fibonacci tuples attain it.
nodes.label: boundDiag

nodes.name: Reduction lemma: some entry is the sum of its neighbours
nodes.statement: If an $n$-tuple $(a_1, a_2,\dots,a_n)$ of positive integers satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, and $a_n\neq1$, then there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that $a_i=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$.
assumptions: an $n$-tuple $(a_1, a_2,\dots,a_n)$ of positive integers satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}
conclusions: there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that $a_i=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$
nodes.label: lem:reductioncases

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.6
nodes.statement:
If there is no such $i$, the condition {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} gives us that $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\geq 2a_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$. Thus, we have
    $a_{i+1}-a_i=a_{i+1}+a_{i-1}-a_{i-1}-a_i\geq a_i - a_{i-1}$ for each $i$.
    Combining these inequalities, and recalling that $a_0=1$, we obtain 
    $$a_{n+1} - a_{n} \geq a_{n} -a_{n-1} \geq \cdots \geq a_2 - a_1 \geq a_1 - a_0 \geq 0.$$
    This implies $a_{n+1} - a_{n} = 1 - a_n \geq 0$, so $a_n=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: otherwise consecutive differences are nondecreasing from $a_1-a_0\ge0$, forcing $a_n=1$.

nodes.name: u_n
nodes.statement: We write $u_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} u_{A_n}$.

nodes.name: Small cases u_1 = 2 and u_2 = 3
nodes.statement: We have $u_1 = 2$ and $u_2=3$.
nodes.label: lem:smolfrieze

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement:
When $n=1$, each diagonal of a frieze is a $1$-tuple $(a_1)$ such that $a_1$ divides $a_0 + a_2 = 1+1=2$. Hence $a_1= 1$ or $2$ and $u_1 \leq 2$. On the other hand, Figure \ref{fig:frieze-width1} implies that $u_1 \geq 2$, and so $u_1 =2$. 

    When $n=2$, each diagonal of a frieze is a pair of integers $(a_1,a_2)$ satisfying condition (\ref{cond:flute}). Applying Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases}, if $a_2=1$, then $a_1$ is $1$ or $2$. When $a_2\neq1$, either $a_1 = 1+a_2$ or $a_2 = 1+a_1$. In the case of the former, $a_2$ divides $1+a_1= 2+a_2$ implies $a_2=2$ and $a_1=3$. A symmetric argument yields $a_1=2$ and $a_2=3$ in the latter case. Thus $u_2 \leq 3$. To conclude, note that Figure \ref{fig:frieze-width2} is a frieze pattern of width $2$ containing the number $3$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the divisibility condition for $n=1,2$, with explicit friezes attaining the bounds.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement:
We prove (1) by induction on $n$. The base cases $n=1$ and $n=2$ are proved in Lemma \ref{lem:smolfrieze}.
    Fix $n \geq 3$, and 
    suppose our claim holds for all $m < n$. Consider an 
    arbitrary $n$-tuple $(a_1,\ldots, a_n)$ satisfying {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}. If $a_n = 1$, one sees that $(a_1,\ldots, a_{n-1})$ is an $(n-1)$-tuple satisfying {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, so by the inductive hypothesis, $a_i \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$, and we are done. If $a_n \neq 1$, there exists by 
    Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases} an index $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$. In this case, $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_i$ and $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$, so $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_{i+1}$. Similarly, $a_{i+1}$ divides $a_{i-1}+a_{i+2}$. In other words the $(n-1)$-tuple 
    \begin{equation} (a_1,\ldots, a_{i-1},\widehat{a}_i, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_n)
    \end{equation}
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} --- here $\widehat{\cdot}$ denotes omission. By induction, $a_k \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $k \in \{1,\ldots , n\} \backslash \{i\}$. It now remains to show that $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$. Applying the above case analysis to the $(n-1)$-tuple given in \eqref{eq:(n-1)diag}, we  conclude that there exists an index $j \in \{1,\ldots, n\} \backslash \{i\}$ such that the 
    $(n-2)$-tuple 
    \[
    (a_1,\ldots,\widehat{a}_i, \ldots, \widehat{a}_j,\ldots,  a_n)
    \]
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, and so $a_k \leq F_n$ for all $k\in \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus \{i,j\}$. If $j = i+1$ or $i-1$, then $$a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \leq F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}.$$ Otherwise, $a_i \leq 2 F_n \leq F_{n+2}$. In either case, $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$, completing the proof of (1).

    The proofs of (2) and (3) are a straightforward 
    computation. The key is to notice that away from the middle of the tuple, we have that
    $$F_{i-2} + F_{i+2} = F_{i-2} + F_{i} + F_{i+1} = F_{i-2} + 2F_{i} + F_{i-1} = 3F_i$$ is divisible by $F_i$. Near the middle of the tuple, the condition (\ref{cond:flute}) is immediate.
nodes.statement_short: Strong induction on $n$: remove an entry equal to its neighbours' sum (Lemma 2.6) and bound it via two smaller tuples. (2),(3) follow from $F_{i-2}+F_{i+2}=3F_i$.

nodes.name: Frieze pattern of type C_n
nodes.statement_short: A $C_n$ frieze satisfies the $A$-type diamond rule except the last row, where $f(n,m)f(n,m+1)=1+f(n-1,m+1)^2$.
nodes.label: def:friezeCn

nodes.name: Type C_n exchange rule
nodes.label: eqn:Cn-rule

nodes.name: Folding friezes of type A_{2n-1} to type C_n
nodes.statement:
Let $a \in {\rm Frieze}(A_{2n-1})$, and suppose that for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$,
\begin{equation} a(n+j,m) = a(n-j,m+j), \quad j \in \{1,\ldots ,n-1\}.
\end{equation}
Then the function $c : \{1,\ldots, n\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ given by 
\begin{equation} c(n-i,m) = a(n-i,-m+i), \quad i \in \{0,\ldots, n-1\}, m \in \mathbb{Z},
\end{equation}
is a frieze pattern of type $C_n$. Moreover, every frieze pattern of type $C_n$ arises in this way.

nodes.name: Symmetry condition on A_{2n-1} frieze
nodes.statement: a(n+j,m) = a(n-j,m+j), \quad j \in \{1,\ldots ,n-1\}.
nodes.label: eq:an-to-cn1

nodes.name: Folded C_n frieze
nodes.statement: c(n-i,m) = a(n-i,-m+i), \quad i \in \{0,\ldots, n-1\}, m \in \mathbb{Z},
nodes.label: eq:an-to-cn2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.10
nodes.statement:
To prove the first claim, it is sufficient to show that the function $c$ thus defined satisfies \eqref{eqn:Cn-rule} for all indices. Let $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ be arbitrary. We proceed by a case-by-case check on the index $i$. 

    {\bf Case 1:} Suppose that $i \in \{1,\ldots, n-1\}$. Set $k = n-i$, so that $k \in \{1,\ldots, n-1\}$.  
    \begin{align*}
    c(k,m) \; c(k,m+1) &= a(k,-m+i)\;  a(k, -(m+1)+i) \\
    &= 1 + a(k+1,-(m+1)+i) \; a(k-1,-m+i) \\
    &= 1 + a(n-(i-1),-m+(i-1)) \, a (n-(i+1),-(m+1)+(i+1)) \\
    & = 1 + c (k+1,m)\; c(k-1,m+1).
    \end{align*}

    {\bf Case 2:} Suppose that $i = 0$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
        c (n,m) \, c(n,m+1) &= a(n,-m) \, a (n, -m-1) \\
        &= 1 + a (n+1,-m-1) \, a(n-1,-m) \\
        &= 1 + a(n+1,-m-1) \, a (n-1,-m-1 +1) \\
        &= 1 + a(n-1,-(m+1)+1)^2, \\
        &= 1 + c(n-1,m+1)^2,
    \end{align*}
    where in the penultimate line we have used the assumption  in the statement of the Lemma. This concludes the proof that every $A_{2n-1}$ frieze pattern gives rise to a $C_n$ frieze. To see that the reverse hold, let $c \in {\rm Frieze}(C_n)$, and define 
    \[
        a : \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0},
    \]
    via the conditions \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1} and \eqref{eq:an-to-cn2}. To show that the resulting function satisfies \eqref{eqn:diamond}, we again proceed by cases on $i \in \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$. 
    
    {\bf Case 1:} $i \in \{1,\ldots, n-1\}$. Set $k = n-i \in \{1,\ldots, n-1\}$. Then,
    \begin{align*}
        a (i,m) \, a(i,m+1) &= a (n-k,m) \, a(n-k,m+1) \\
        &=  a (n-k,-(-m+k)+k) \, a(n-k,-(-m-1+k)+k) \\
        &=  c (n-k,-m+k) \, c(n-k,-m+k-1)\\
        &= 1 + c(n-k+1,-m+k-1) \, c(n-k-1,-m+k)\\
        &= 1 + c (n - (k-1), -m+k-1) \, c(n - (k+1),-m+k) \\
        &= 1 + a (i+1,m) \, a (i-1,m+1).
    \end{align*}
    
    {\bf Case 2:} $i = n$. Then,
    \begin{align*}
        a (n,m) \, a(n,m+1) &= c (n,-m) \, c(n,-m-1) \\
        &= 1 + c(n-1,-m)^2 \\
        &= 1 + a (n-1,m+1)^2 \\
        &= 1 + a (n+1,m)\, a (n-1,m+1).
    \end{align*}

    The remaining case $i \in \{n+1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$ reduces to the first case via \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1}, and we omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Case-by-case verification of the exchange relations, in both directions, via the reindexing (9)-(10).

nodes.name: Folded frieze of type C_3
nodes.statement:
The following is the frieze pattern of type $C_3$ obtained from the frieze of type $A_5$ given in Example \ref{ex:friezeA5} via Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn}. 
    \[
\begin{matrix}
    1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1  \\
    & 3 && 3 && 2 && 1 && 3 && 3  && 2 \\
   \cdots && 8 && 5 && 1 && 2 && 8 && 5 && 1 && \cdots  \\
    &&& 13 && 2 && 1 && 5 && 13 && 2 && 1  \\
    &&&&1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1 && 1
\end{matrix}
\]
nodes.label: ex:foldedC3

nodes.name: Regular polygon P_{n+3}
nodes.statement: Consider the regular polygon $P_{n+3}$ with $(n+3)$ vertices (labelled cyclically by $\{1,\ldots, n+3\}$) and $(n+3)$ edges.

nodes.name: Diagonal of a polygon
nodes.statement: We call a {\it diagonal} any pair $\{i,j\}$ of non-consecutive vertices.

nodes.name: Intersecting diagonals
nodes.statement:
We say that two diagonals $(i_1,i_2)$ and $(j_1,j_2)$ {\it intersect} if $i_1= j_1$ and $i_2 = j_2$, or if
\[
    i_1<j_1<i_2<j_2, \text{ or } j_1<i_1<j_2<i_2.
\]

nodes.name: Non-intersecting diagonals
nodes.statement: Otherwise, the two diagonals are said to be {\it non-intersecting}.

nodes.name: Triangulation of a polygon
nodes.statement: A {\it triangulation} of $P_{n+3}$ is any maximal (w.r.t. inclusion) collection of (pairwise) non-intersecting diagonals.

nodes.name: Triangulation has n diagonals
nodes.statement: Each triangulation contains exactly $n$ diagonals.
conclusions: Each triangulation contains exactly $n$ diagonals.

nodes.name: Conway-Coxeter correspondence friezes-triangulations
nodes.statement: By \cite{CC73}, there is a one-to-one correspondence between frieze patterns of type $A_n$ and triangulations of $P_{n+3}$ (see Remark \ref{eq:zigzag} for an example of a triangulation).
conclusions: there is a one-to-one correspondence between frieze patterns of type $A_n$ and triangulations of $P_{n+3}$

nodes.name: Fontaine-Plamondon: C_n friezes and centrally symmetric triangulations
nodes.statement: According to the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.2]{FP:Dn}, frieze patterns of type $C_n$ are in one-to-one correspondence (using the algebraic procedure from Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn}) with frieze patterns of type $A_{2n-1}$ coming from triangulations of $P_{2n+2}$ that are symmetric under central symmetry, i.e. the symmetry which sends the vertex $i$ to the vertex $i + n+1$.
conclusions: frieze patterns of type $C_n$ are in one-to-one correspondence (using the algebraic procedure from Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn}) with frieze patterns of type $A_{2n-1}$ coming from triangulations of $P_{2n+2}$ that are symmetric under central symmetry
nodes.statement_short: $C_n$ friezes correspond to $A_{2n-1}$ friezes from centrally symmetric triangulations of $P_{2n+2}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (2)
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn} and statement (1) of Theorem \ref{mainthm}, we have $u_{C_n} \leq u_{A_{2n-1}} = F_{2n+1}$. It remains to show that there exists a frieze pattern of type $C_n$ that realises this upper bound. By Remark \ref{eq:zigzag} and the discussion following Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn}, it is sufficient to show that the zig-zag triangulation of $P_{2n+2}$ is symmetric under the symmetry sending the vertex $i$ to the vertex $i + n+1$. One checks directly that diagonal of the zig-zag triangulation is of the form $(2+i,2n+2-i)$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n-2$ or $(2+i+1,2n+2-i)$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n-3$, and that the set of diagonals in this triangulation is indeed preserved. 
The resulting frieze pattern of type $C_n$, denoted $c$, satisfies $c(i,0) = F_{2i+1}$ for $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$ (see Figure \ref{ex:foldedC3} for the case $n= 3$). \qed
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from folding and part (1); the bound is attained by the centrally symmetric zig-zag triangulation of $P_{2n+2}$.

nodes.name: Assume no such $i$; then $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\ge 2a_i$
nodes.statement: If there is no such $i$, the condition {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} gives us that $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\geq 2a_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume no such $i$; then $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\ge 2a_i$

nodes.name: Differences are nondecreasing
nodes.statement:
Thus, we have
    $a_{i+1}-a_i=a_{i+1}+a_{i-1}-a_{i-1}-a_i\geq a_i - a_{i-1}$ for each $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Differences are nondecreasing

nodes.name: Chain the inequalities down to $a_1-a_0\ge0$
nodes.statement:
Combining these inequalities, and recalling that $a_0=1$, we obtain 
    $$a_{n+1} - a_{n} \geq a_{n} -a_{n-1} \geq \cdots \geq a_2 - a_1 \geq a_1 - a_0 \geq 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Chain the inequalities down to $a_1-a_0\ge0$

nodes.name: Conclude $a_n=1$, a contradiction
nodes.statement: This implies $a_{n+1} - a_{n} = 1 - a_n \geq 0$, so $a_n=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $a_n=1$, a contradiction

nodes.name: Case $n=1$: $u_1=2$
nodes.statement: When $n=1$, each diagonal of a frieze is a $1$-tuple $(a_1)$ such that $a_1$ divides $a_0 + a_2 = 1+1=2$. Hence $a_1= 1$ or $2$ and $u_1 \leq 2$. On the other hand, Figure \ref{fig:frieze-width1} implies that $u_1 \geq 2$, and so $u_1 =2$.

nodes.name: Case $n=2$: via Lemma 2.6, $u_2=3$
nodes.statement: When $n=2$, each diagonal of a frieze is a pair of integers $(a_1,a_2)$ satisfying condition (\ref{cond:flute}). Applying Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases}, if $a_2=1$, then $a_1$ is $1$ or $2$. When $a_2\neq1$, either $a_1 = 1+a_2$ or $a_2 = 1+a_1$. In the case of the former, $a_2$ divides $1+a_1= 2+a_2$ implies $a_2=2$ and $a_1=3$. A symmetric argument yields $a_1=2$ and $a_2=3$ in the latter case. Thus $u_2 \leq 3$. To conclude, note that Figure \ref{fig:frieze-width2} is a frieze pattern of width $2$ containing the number $3$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $n=2$: via Lemma 2.6, $u_2=3$

nodes.name: Prove (1) by strong induction on $n$
nodes.statement:
We prove (1) by induction on $n$. The base cases $n=1$ and $n=2$ are proved in Lemma \ref{lem:smolfrieze}.
    Fix $n \geq 3$, and 
    suppose our claim holds for all $m < n$. Consider an 
    arbitrary $n$-tuple $(a_1,\ldots, a_n)$ satisfying {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}. If $a_n = 1$, one sees that $(a_1,\ldots, a_{n-1})$ is an $(n-1)$-tuple satisfying {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, so by the inductive hypothesis, $a_i \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$, and we are done. If $a_n \neq 1$, there exists by 
    Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases} an index $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$. In this case, $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_i$ and $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$, so $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_{i+1}$. Similarly, $a_{i+1}$ divides $a_{i-1}+a_{i+2}$. In other words the $(n-1)$-tuple 
    \begin{equation} (a_1,\ldots, a_{i-1},\widehat{a}_i, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_n)
    \end{equation}
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} --- here $\widehat{\cdot}$ denotes omission. By induction, $a_k \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $k \in \{1,\ldots , n\} \backslash \{i\}$. It now remains to show that $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$. Applying the above case analysis to the $(n-1)$-tuple given in \eqref{eq:(n-1)diag}, we  conclude that there exists an index $j \in \{1,\ldots, n\} \backslash \{i\}$ such that the 
    $(n-2)$-tuple 
    \[
    (a_1,\ldots,\widehat{a}_i, \ldots, \widehat{a}_j,\ldots,  a_n)
    \]
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, and so $a_k \leq F_n$ for all $k\in \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus \{i,j\}$. If $j = i+1$ or $i-1$, then $$a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \leq F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}.$$ Otherwise, $a_i \leq 2 F_n \leq F_{n+2}$. In either case, $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$, completing the proof of (1).
nodes.statement_short: Prove (1) by strong induction on $n$

nodes.name: Base cases $n=1,2$ from Lemma 2.7
nodes.statement: We prove (1) by induction on $n$. The base cases $n=1$ and $n=2$ are proved in Lemma \ref{lem:smolfrieze}.
nodes.statement_short: Base cases $n=1,2$ from Lemma 2.7

nodes.name: Fix $n\ge3$ with the induction hypothesis and an arbitrary tuple satisfying (*)
nodes.statement_short: Fix $n\ge3$ with the induction hypothesis and an arbitrary tuple satisfying (*)

nodes.name: Case $a_n=1$: drop $a_n$ and use induction
nodes.statement: If $a_n = 1$, one sees that $(a_1,\ldots, a_{n-1})$ is an $(n-1)$-tuple satisfying {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, so by the inductive hypothesis, $a_i \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Case $a_n=1$: drop $a_n$ and use induction

nodes.name: Case $a_n\ne1$: remove an entry equal to its neighbours' sum
nodes.statement:
If $a_n \neq 1$, there exists by 
    Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases} an index $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$. In this case, $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_i$ and $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$, so $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_{i+1}$. Similarly, $a_{i+1}$ divides $a_{i-1}+a_{i+2}$. In other words the $(n-1)$-tuple 
    \begin{equation} (a_1,\ldots, a_{i-1},\widehat{a}_i, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_n)
    \end{equation}
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} --- here $\widehat{\cdot}$ denotes omission. By induction, $a_k \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $k \in \{1,\ldots , n\} \backslash \{i\}$. It now remains to show that $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$. Applying the above case analysis to the $(n-1)$-tuple given in \eqref{eq:(n-1)diag}, we  conclude that there exists an index $j \in \{1,\ldots, n\} \backslash \{i\}$ such that the 
    $(n-2)$-tuple 
    \[
    (a_1,\ldots,\widehat{a}_i, \ldots, \widehat{a}_j,\ldots,  a_n)
    \]
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, and so $a_k \leq F_n$ for all $k\in \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus \{i,j\}$. If $j = i+1$ or $i-1$, then $$a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1} \leq F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}.$$ Otherwise, $a_i \leq 2 F_n \leq F_{n+2}$. In either case, $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$, completing the proof of (1).
nodes.statement_short: Case $a_n\ne1$: remove an entry equal to its neighbours' sum

nodes.name: Lemma 2.6 gives $a_i=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$; deleting $a_i$ keeps (*)
nodes.statement:
If $a_n \neq 1$, there exists by 
    Lemma \ref{lem:reductioncases} an index $i \in \{1,\ldots , n\}$ such that $a_i = a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$. In this case, $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_i$ and $a_i = a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$, so $a_{i-1}$ divides $a_{i-2}+a_{i+1}$. Similarly, $a_{i+1}$ divides $a_{i-1}+a_{i+2}$. In other words the $(n-1)$-tuple 
    \begin{equation} (a_1,\ldots, a_{i-1},\widehat{a}_i, a_{i+1}, \ldots, a_n)
    \end{equation}
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}} --- here $\widehat{\cdot}$ denotes omission.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.6 gives $a_i=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$; deleting $a_i$ keeps (*)

nodes.name: Induction bounds all entries except $a_i$
nodes.statement: By induction, $a_k \leq F_{n+1} \leq F_{n+2}$ for all $k \in \{1,\ldots , n\} \backslash \{i\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction bounds all entries except $a_i$

nodes.name: Remains to bound $a_i$
nodes.statement: It now remains to show that $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to bound $a_i$

nodes.name: Delete a second entry $a_j$; induction gives $a_k\le F_n$ off $\{i,j\}$
nodes.statement:
Applying the above case analysis to the $(n-1)$-tuple given in \eqref{eq:(n-1)diag}, we  conclude that there exists an index $j \in \{1,\ldots, n\} \backslash \{i\}$ such that the 
    $(n-2)$-tuple 
    \[
    (a_1,\ldots,\widehat{a}_i, \ldots, \widehat{a}_j,\ldots,  a_n)
    \]
    satisfies {\normalfont{(\ref{cond:flute})}}, and so $a_k \leq F_n$ for all $k\in \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus \{i,j\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Delete a second entry $a_j$; induction gives $a_k\le F_n$ off $\{i,j\}$

nodes.name: If $j$ adjacent to $i$: $a_i\le F_{n+1}+F_n$
nodes.statement_short: If $j$ adjacent to $i$: $a_i\le F_{n+1}+F_n$

nodes.name: Otherwise $a_i\le 2F_n$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $a_i \leq 2 F_n \leq F_{n+2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $a_i\le 2F_n$

nodes.name: Conclude $a_i\le F_{n+2}$
nodes.statement: In either case, $a_i \leq F_{n+2}$, completing the proof of (1).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $a_i\le F_{n+2}$

nodes.name: Parts (2),(3): use $F_{i-2}+F_{i+2}=3F_i$
nodes.statement:
The proofs of (2) and (3) are a straightforward 
    computation. The key is to notice that away from the middle of the tuple, we have that
    $$F_{i-2} + F_{i+2} = F_{i-2} + F_{i} + F_{i+1} = F_{i-2} + 2F_{i} + F_{i-1} = 3F_i$$ is divisible by $F_i$. Near the middle of the tuple, the condition (\ref{cond:flute}) is immediate.

nodes.name: Reduce to checking (8) for $c$, case by case on $i$
nodes.statement: To prove the first claim, it is sufficient to show that the function $c$ thus defined satisfies \eqref{eqn:Cn-rule} for all indices. Let $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ be arbitrary. We proceed by a case-by-case check on the index $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to checking (8) for $c$, case by case on $i$

nodes.name: Case $i\ge1$: exchange relation for $c$ from that of $a$
nodes.statement_short: Case $i\ge1$: exchange relation for $c$ from that of $a$

nodes.name: Case $i=0$ via symmetry; then begin the converse
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 2:} Suppose that $i = 0$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
        c (n,m) \, c(n,m+1) &= a(n,-m) \, a (n, -m-1) \\
        &= 1 + a (n+1,-m-1) \, a(n-1,-m) \\
        &= 1 + a(n+1,-m-1) \, a (n-1,-m-1 +1) \\
        &= 1 + a(n-1,-(m+1)+1)^2, \\
        &= 1 + c(n-1,m+1)^2,
    \end{align*}
    where in the penultimate line we have used the assumption  in the statement of the Lemma. This concludes the proof that every $A_{2n-1}$ frieze pattern gives rise to a $C_n$ frieze. To see that the reverse hold, let $c \in {\rm Frieze}(C_n)$, and define 
    \[
        a : \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0},
    \]
    via the conditions \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1} and \eqref{eq:an-to-cn2}. To show that the resulting function satisfies \eqref{eqn:diamond}, we again proceed by cases on $i \in \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $i=0$ via symmetry; then begin the converse

nodes.name: Last-row relation for $c$ using the symmetry assumption (9)
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 2:} Suppose that $i = 0$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
        c (n,m) \, c(n,m+1) &= a(n,-m) \, a (n, -m-1) \\
        &= 1 + a (n+1,-m-1) \, a(n-1,-m) \\
        &= 1 + a(n+1,-m-1) \, a (n-1,-m-1 +1) \\
        &= 1 + a(n-1,-(m+1)+1)^2, \\
        &= 1 + c(n-1,m+1)^2,
    \end{align*}
    where in the penultimate line we have used the assumption  in the statement of the Lemma. This concludes the proof that every $A_{2n-1}$ frieze pattern gives rise to a $C_n$ frieze.
nodes.statement_short: Last-row relation for $c$ using the symmetry assumption (9)

nodes.name: Converse: define $a$ from $c$ via (9),(10)
nodes.statement:
To see that the reverse hold, let $c \in {\rm Frieze}(C_n)$, and define 
    \[
        a : \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\} \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0},
    \]
    via the conditions \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1} and \eqref{eq:an-to-cn2}.
nodes.statement_short: Converse: define $a$ from $c$ via (9),(10)

nodes.name: Check the diamond rule for $a$ by cases
nodes.statement: To show that the resulting function satisfies \eqref{eqn:diamond}, we again proceed by cases on $i \in \{1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the diamond rule for $a$ by cases

nodes.name: Case $i\le n-1$ for $a$
nodes.statement_short: Case $i\le n-1$ for $a$

nodes.name: Case $i=n$, and remaining cases by symmetry
nodes.statement:
{\bf Case 2:} $i = n$. Then,
    \begin{align*}
        a (n,m) \, a(n,m+1) &= c (n,-m) \, c(n,-m-1) \\
        &= 1 + c(n-1,-m)^2 \\
        &= 1 + a (n-1,m+1)^2 \\
        &= 1 + a (n+1,m)\, a (n-1,m+1).
    \end{align*}

    The remaining case $i \in \{n+1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$ reduces to the first case via \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1}, and we omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Case $i=n$, and remaining cases by symmetry

nodes.name: Middle-row relation for $a$
nodes.statement_short: Middle-row relation for $a$

nodes.name: Cases $i>n$ reduce to Case 1 by (9)
nodes.statement: The remaining case $i \in \{n+1,\ldots, 2n-1\}$ reduces to the first case via \eqref{eq:an-to-cn1}, and we omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Cases $i>n$ reduce to Case 1 by (9)

nodes.name: Upper bound $u_{C_n}\le u_{A_{2n-1}}=F_{2n+1}$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn} and statement (1) of Theorem \ref{mainthm}, we have $u_{C_n} \leq u_{A_{2n-1}} = F_{2n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound $u_{C_n}\le u_{A_{2n-1}}=F_{2n+1}$

nodes.name: Remains to realise the bound
nodes.statement: It remains to show that there exists a frieze pattern of type $C_n$ that realises this upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to realise the bound

nodes.name: Reduce to central symmetry of the zig-zag triangulation
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{eq:zigzag} and the discussion following Lemma \ref{l:foldingAnCn}, it is sufficient to show that the zig-zag triangulation of $P_{2n+2}$ is symmetric under the symmetry sending the vertex $i$ to the vertex $i + n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to central symmetry of the zig-zag triangulation

nodes.name: Check the zig-zag diagonals are preserved by the symmetry
nodes.statement: One checks directly that diagonal of the zig-zag triangulation is of the form $(2+i,2n+2-i)$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n-2$ or $(2+i+1,2n+2-i)$ for $i = 0, \ldots, n-3$, and that the set of diagonals in this triangulation is indeed preserved.
nodes.statement_short: Check the zig-zag diagonals are preserved by the symmetry

nodes.name: Resulting $C_n$ frieze has $c(i,0)=F_{2i+1}$
nodes.statement: The resulting frieze pattern of type $C_n$, denoted $c$, satisfies $c(i,0) = F_{2i+1}$ for $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\}$ (see Figure \ref{ex:foldedC3} for the case $n= 3$). \qed
nodes.statement_short: Resulting $C_n$ frieze has $c(i,0)=F_{2i+1}$
